intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself against the questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What Academic Writing Is For
sections.big_idea: Academic writing is **an argument made checkable**: a claim, the evidence for it, and enough for a stranger to disagree.
in_plain_words: Many writers think academic prose means long words, passive verbs and hedged sentences. The deck says those add nothing. What makes writing academic is the contract: a claim, the evidence and reasoning behind it, a place among what others found, and room for the reader to disagree.

The contract stays the same across a thesis, an article, a working paper and a policy brief. Length, reader and the amount of checking apparatus change. So the first job is to pick the genre and write for its reader, who is **busy, sceptical and not you**.
Drafting is the short part of the work. A paper that takes three months to write can take two years to publish, so plan a pipeline of papers at different stages.

diagram.caption: five things a reader should be able to check

key_terms.meaning: Prose that makes a claim and shows the evidence and reasoning so every step can be checked.
A type of document, such as an article or policy brief, with its own reader and length.
Forgetting what it was like not to know what you now know.
Papers at different stages at once: under review, in revision, in draft.
The English many South Asian researchers write; plain sentences read well in it.

worked_example.title: Turn a thesis chapter into an article
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: your thesis chapter has 9,000 words, and 3,000 of them are literature review that the journal does not want.
steps: Name the new reader: specialists who will check the method, in an article of 6,000 to 10,000 words.
Cut the literature the journal does not want: 9,000 − 3,000 = 6,000 words.
6,000 words sits at the bottom of the article range, so check that the claim and replication detail survived the cut.
A policy brief for the same study would be a separate document of 2 to 6 pages, with the recommendation first.
worked_example.answer: 6,000 words remain, enough for an article; the brief is written separately.

mistakes: Writing one document and relabelling it for another genre, which leaves a thesis review in an article or buries a recommendation on page nine.
Using long words and hedged sentences to sound academic when the contract is checkable claims.
Assuming the reader knows your abbreviations and your district because you do.
Drafting a single paper at a time, which leaves the pipeline empty for years.

recall.q: What is the distinguishing feature of academic writing?
recall.a: Every step of the argument can be checked.

recall.q: In which order does the deck say a reader meets a paper?
recall.a: Title, abstract, first figure and conclusion.

recall.q: How long is Belcher's plan from draft to submitted article?
recall.a: Twelve weeks, at about an hour a day.

recall.q: What is the cure for the curse of knowledge?
recall.a: A reader outside the sub-field who marks every sentence they had to read twice.

recall.q: What is the common thread across the two bad models?
recall.a: Neither shows its reasoning in a form a stranger can check.

sections.title: The Argument
sections.big_idea: A topic becomes a question, then a claim, then a **so what**; the claim is written before the paper.
in_plain_words: Most stalled drafts sit at the topic or the question. A topic has no natural end, a question ends when it is answered, and a claim can be defended. Write one sentence on a card: this paper shows that X, because Y, which matters for Z. If you cannot write it, the analysis is unfinished.

The claim then needs a type of contribution, such as a finding, an estimate, a mechanism or a measure. Its shape follows an hourglass: wide on the problem, narrow through data and results, wide again on meaning. The main result and its number belong in the introduction.

The claim is only as strong as the best objection it survives, so list the referee's objections first and answer them in named paragraphs. Title, abstract, introduction and conclusion then carry the claim to the places readers look first.

diagram.caption: the four steps from subject to significance

key_terms.meaning: The sentence the paper defends, with a number where possible.
The question the reader asks whether or not you answer it.
Wide on the problem, narrow in data and results, wide on meaning.
What the paper adds: finding, estimate, mechanism, measure, method, synthesis or theory.
The argument that an estimate shows a cause, which a referee tests.

worked_example.title: Size a claim against a control mean
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: your claim is that SHG membership raises the share of decisions women make alone by 8 points, and the control mean is 32 percent.
steps: The deck suggests giving the scale of an effect, such as a share of the control mean.
Divide the effect by the control mean: 8 ÷ 32 = 0.25.
So the effect is a quarter of the control mean.
Write the claim card: this paper shows that membership raises decision share by 8 points, because of savings, which matters for programme design.
worked_example.answer: The 8 points equal a quarter of the control mean, and that goes in the claim.

mistakes: Starting a paper from a topic and waiting for the argument to appear.
Calling an application of a standard method to a new dataset a contribution with no reason the answer would differ.
Holding the main result back for suspense instead of stating it in the introduction.
Answering an objection with 'we acknowledge this limitation' and no analysis.

recall.q: What sentence does the claim card contain?
recall.a: This paper shows that X, because Y, which matters for Z.

recall.q: Name three kinds of contribution.
recall.a: Any three of: finding, better estimate, mechanism, measurement, method, synthesis, theory or framework.

recall.q: Where must the main result appear whatever the field?
recall.a: In the introduction, with its number.

recall.q: How long should an abstract be?
recall.a: 150 to 250 words.

recall.q: Which introduction paragraph decides most rejections?
recall.a: Paragraph 6, the contribution against named papers.

sections.title: Structure
sections.big_idea: Use **the shape of the journal you are sending to**, and outline before drafting so structural faults are cheap to fix.
in_plain_words: IMRaD, the health default, has four parts. Economics keeps them and renames them, and development studies adds a context section. None is better than the others, so read your target journal and copy its shape.

Whatever the headings, the reader must find the sample size, comparison group, main estimate and confidence interval within a minute. Setting, data, methods, results and discussion each owe the reader specific things, listed in the slides.

An outline of headings with a one-sentence claim under each is finished before the prose begins. After a draft, reverse-outline it. For a thesis, decide between monograph and three papers in year one.

diagram.caption: a typical empirical paper, top to bottom

key_terms.meaning: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, the health-science default.
The programme and place facts the argument and interpretation depend on.
Data or instructions plus code, README and software versions.
One sentence beside each paragraph saying what it does.
Unlimited space for checks and tables a general reader skips.

worked_example.title: Budget the words in an outline
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an 8,000-word article, within the 6,000 to 10,000 range the deck gives for journals.
steps: Give each section a word budget in the outline, and decide overruns consciously.
Allocate: introduction 1,500, setting 800, data 1,000, methods 1,200, results 1,800, discussion 1,200, conclusion 500.
Write each heading as a claim, such as 'The effect runs through savings'.
worked_example.answer: The budget totals 8,000 words with every section assigned.

mistakes: Writing a setting section as tourism, with facts nothing later refers back to.
Describing methods in one sentence, such as 'thematic analysis was conducted', when a page is owed.
Putting a robustness check that changes the answer in the appendix.
Changing a thesis from monograph to three papers in year four.

recall.q: What does IMRaD stand for?
recall.a: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion.

recall.q: What three parts does a quantitative methods section need?
recall.a: The equation, the assumption and the test of the assumption.

recall.q: Which check stays in the paper, and which goes to the appendix?
recall.a: The one check that changes the answer stays; confirming checks go to the appendix.

recall.q: When should the thesis form be decided?
recall.a: In year one, with the supervisor, in writing.

recall.q: What does reverse outlining find?
recall.a: Structural problems that reading the prose hides.

sections.title: The Literature Review
sections.big_idea: A review is **an argument about the literature**: what is settled, what is disputed, what is missing and why it matters.
in_plain_words: The annotated bibliography, one paragraph per paper, is the commonest failure in Indian theses. A review is organised by theme, finding or method, and each paragraph makes a claim about the literature and cites the papers that support it.

To build it, read in three passes (triage, structure, close) and record each paper in a fixed set of fields. A synthesis matrix with one row per study lets structure appear when you sort a column. Then write each theme in three moves: group, explain, position.

Include reports, working papers and government documents, appraised like papers. A theory chapter must change what the empirical chapters do. Set up alerts and Zotero early so the review is current at submission.

diagram.caption: repeat the three moves for every theme

key_terms.meaning: A structured account of evidence organised by theme, ending on what this study adds.
A table with one row per study and one column per theme.
Reports, working papers and agency documents outside journals.
An annotated bibliography presented as a review.
A free reference manager that stores papers, notes and citations.

worked_example.title: Group, explain, position
worked_example.setup: Four randomised studies of SHG programmes measure women's decision-making, as in the deck's example.
steps: Group: three find positive effects of 5 to 12 points and one finds none, so 4 − 3 = 1 null result.
Explain: the null comes from the only study whose groups had no savings component.
Position: none of the four separates savings from credit; your study does, using staggered introduction of credit across blocks.
End the theme on the gap as a question your data can answer.
worked_example.answer: One null among four, explained by the missing savings component, and a specific gap for your study.

mistakes: Organising the review by author or by the order you read the papers.
Citing a paper for what a textbook says it says, instead of reading the primary source.
Treating grey literature as equal to peer-reviewed work without appraising it.
Summarising three theories in a framework chapter and using none of them.

recall.q: What are the three reading passes?
recall.a: Triage, structure and close.

recall.q: What are the three synthesis moves?
recall.a: Group, explain and position.

recall.q: How should a review end?
recall.a: On the gap, stated as a question your data can answer.

recall.q: What is 'According to government data'?
recall.a: Not a citation; give the issuing body, title, year and table.

recall.q: How often does the deck suggest spending time on keeping the review current?
recall.a: One hour a fortnight.

sections.title: Sentences and Paragraphs
sections.big_idea: Clear sentences have **a character as subject and an action as verb**, with new information at the end.
in_plain_words: Williams and Bizup reduce clarity to two rules: make the main characters the grammatical subjects, and make their actions the verbs. Nominalisations such as implementation and utilisation hide the verb, so turn them back.

Readers expect old information at the start and new information at the end. Each paragraph carries one claim, its support, any qualification and a link forward. Skimming the first sentences should give the whole argument.

Hedge exactly as much as the evidence allows, cut filler words after the first draft, define jargon once, and draft and revise on different days. Ask readers for specific comments and use the right tool for your field.

diagram.note: 'Enrolment rose after the transfer began' has all three

key_terms.meaning: A verb turned into a noun, such as utilisation for use.
The start of a sentence, where readers expect what it is about.
The end of a sentence, where new or important information goes.
A verb choice that matches claim strength to evidence strength.
A one-sentence-per-paragraph check of structure.

worked_example.title: Cut a sentence and a draft
worked_example.setup: The deck's before sentence has 33 words; the after sentence has 13. Illustrative: your draft has 8,000 words.
steps: Words removed from the sentence: 33 − 13 = 20.
The after version has a character ('we') and an action ('estimate'), and nothing was lost.
For the draft, cut 10% at the end: 8,000 × 0.10 = 800 words.
Remaining length: 8,000 − 800 = 7,200 words.
worked_example.answer: The sentence loses 20 words; the draft ends at 7,200 words.

mistakes: Putting new information first and trailing off into old information.
Using connective words such as 'in addition' to join paragraphs that have no real link.
Writing 'proves' or 'impact' for a cross-sectional correlation.
Revising sentences while drafting, which gives a beautiful first page and no paper.

recall.q: What are Williams and Bizup's two rules?
recall.a: Make the main characters the subjects and their actions the verbs.

recall.q: How far apart should subject and verb be?
recall.a: Within seven words of each other.

recall.q: Which verb fits a randomised, precise result?
recall.a: Shows, finds, raises or reduces.

recall.q: What are the five revision passes?
recall.a: Draft, structure, argument, sentences and surface.

recall.q: How much does the deck suggest cutting at the end?

sections.title: Numbers, Tables and Figures
sections.big_idea: Round in prose, keep decimals in tables, and give every number **its base, its precision and its scale**.
in_plain_words: Readers cannot compare 8.37 and 6.92 in their heads, but they can compare 8 and 7. Round in the sentence and keep the decimals in the table. Always say whether a change is in percent or percentage points, and give the base.

A table is for looking numbers up; a figure is for seeing a pattern. Tables need a title that says the outcome and sample, a note that makes them readable alone, and columns from sparest to fullest. Figures carry intervals and one message in the title.

Equations are numbered and every symbol is defined after them. Table 1 is the most-read table in a paper. Qualitative evidence needs quotations presented as exhibits with counts. The replication package lets a stranger check every number you report.

key_terms.meaning: The simple difference between two percentages.
The average outcome in the comparison group; effects are read against it.
Table 1 comparing groups before treatment.
Everything needed to reproduce each table and figure.
One test of balance across variables instead of stars on each.

worked_example.title: Percent or percentage points?
worked_example.setup: Enrolment rose from 75% to 81%, the deck's example.
steps: Percentage points: 81 − 75 = 6.
Percent change: 6 ÷ 75 = 0.08, which is 8 percent.
Write both with the base: 6 points, from a control mean of 75%.
Avoid saying 'increased by 200%'; say 'tripled' or give both numbers.
worked_example.answer: Enrolment rose 6 percentage points, which is 8 percent.

mistakes: Reporting 8.37 percentage points in prose when about 8 reads better.
Starring every row of a balance table, so chance differences look meaningful.
Retyping regression numbers by hand instead of generating the table from code.
Dropping the confidence interval from a coefficient plot.

recall.q: How many significant figures in prose?
recall.a: Two.

recall.q: What belongs in a table note?
recall.a: Sample, controls, clustering, significance convention and data source.

recall.q: When does the deck say a pie chart earns its place?
recall.a: Almost never.

recall.q: How should quoted interviews be counted?
recall.a: Say how many said it and who said the opposite.

recall.q: Where do robustness tables that confirm go?
recall.a: In the appendix.

sections.title: Citation and Integrity
sections.big_idea: Citation is **the checking apparatus**; integrity means data, text and permissions are handled with care.
in_plain_words: A citation lets the reader check a claim, credits the person who did the work and places your paper in the literature. Cite what you read, cite the specific work, and cite when in doubt. The journal chooses the style; you control completeness.

The UGC 2018 regulations tier similarity scores from Level 0 to Level 3, but the score only finds matching strings. Plagiarism is the act of presenting another's words, data, ideas or structure as yours, and it can occur at 3% similarity.

Integrity also covers text recycling, salami slicing, duplicate submission, fabrication and falsification. File a pre-analysis plan for confirmatory work, check permissions before reusing figures or tables, and verify every reference against its DOI before you submit.

key_terms.meaning: Changing a few words of a copied paragraph; plagiarism even when cited.
Splitting one study into the smallest publishable papers.
Sending one paper to two journals at once.
Changing data or results, including undisclosed specification search.
A registered plan stating outcomes and specification before data are seen.

worked_example.title: Place four theses on the tiers
worked_example.setup: Illustrative similarity scores for four theses: 8%, 25%, 45% and 65%.
steps: 8% is up to 10%, so Level 0: minor, no penalty.
25% is above 10% to 40%, so Level 1: revised script within six months.
45% is above 40% to 60%, so Level 2: debarred from submitting a revised script for one year.
65% is above 60%, so Level 3: registration cancelled.
worked_example.answer: Level 0, Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 respectively.

mistakes: Taking a low similarity score as proof of originality.
Writing a paraphrase with the source open and calling it your own words.
Reusing an introduction or results section from your own earlier paper without disclosure.
Adding a reference suggested by a language model without checking its DOI.

recall.q: What does the similarity score actually find?
recall.a: Matching strings.

recall.q: What is the safe paraphrase method?
recall.a: Read, close the source, write from memory, then reopen to check and cite.

recall.q: Which quotations are set as a block?
recall.a: Those over forty words.

recall.q: What should you do when unsure about overlap?
recall.a: Disclose it to the editor.

recall.q: What is the last step of the referencing workflow?
recall.a: Verify every reference against its DOI.

sections.title: The Thesis in India
sections.big_idea: Your **university ordinance** governs the thesis, so get it in the first month and read it twice.
in_plain_words: The UGC PhD Regulations 2022 set stages: entry, coursework of at least 12 credits, a Research Advisory Committee, a duration of three to six years, a plagiarism check, evaluation by external examiners, an open viva and deposit on Shodhganga.

Each university writes its own ordinance inside the regulations, and the ordinance sets chapter lists, limits and format. Build your template from it and two recently passed theses. Manage your supervisor with agendas, notes and a record.

Examiners read the abstract, contents, introduction and conclusion first, so the argument must be visible there. The viva is where the work is defended before examiners and the department. Plan the thesis-to-article path in year one so a submitted chapter exists before the viva.

events.what: Decide the form; chapters that become articles
First empirical chapter as article; post it
Revise under review; write thesis intro last

key_terms.meaning: Your university's own rules within the UGC regulations.
Supervisor plus two members who review progress each semester.
Open defence before examiners and the department.
INFLIBNET's public repository of Indian doctoral theses.
The thesis in miniature, required before registration and again before submission.

worked_example.title: How long is the PhD window?
worked_example.setup: The deck gives a minimum of three years including coursework and a maximum of six, extendable.
steps: Take the maximum: 6 years.
Take the minimum: 3 years.
The window for finishing is 6 − 3 = 3 years.
Extensions are the university's decision.
worked_example.answer: A three-year window between minimum and maximum duration.

mistakes: Building a template from memory instead of the ordinance and two passed theses.
Putting a proposal that opens with 'a mixed-methods approach will be adopted' ahead of the question.
Hearing the supervisor's silence on the argument as approval.
Putting participant-identifying detail into a thesis that becomes public on Shodhganga.

recall.q: How many credits of coursework do the 2022 regulations require?
recall.a: A minimum of 12.

recall.q: Is publication before submission mandatory nationally?
recall.a: No, though a university may still require it.

recall.q: What are the four possible examiner recommendations?
recall.a: Award, award after minor corrections, resubmit after major revision, or reject.

recall.q: What should a viva presentation follow?
recall.a: The hourglass: problem, question, design, findings, contribution, limits.

recall.q: What goes in a supervisor meeting note?
recall.a: What was agreed, as the record when memories differ.

sections.title: Choosing and Reaching a Journal
sections.big_idea: Choose by **fit first**, then reach, speed and cost; a paper at the wrong journal is rejected at the desk.
in_plain_words: Shortlist four journals in order and write for the first. Your own reference list and the last two issues tell you where papers like yours appear. Reach comes next: indexing, readers and open access. Since February 2025 India has no national journal list.

Predatory journals show up as flattering invitations, late fees and weak boards. Check DOAJ, Scopus and Web of Science directly. For open access, green plus a preprint is free and compliant for most South Asian authors.

The submission needs a half-page cover letter and anonymisation where review is double-blind. Journal metrics describe journal averages and say nothing about your paper. Timelines run 9 to 18 months from first submission, and longer after a rejection.

diagram.caption: the order of the four questions

key_terms.meaning: Editor's rejection before referees, often for poor fit or format.
An outlet that puts self-interest above scholarship.
You post the accepted manuscript on a repository after an embargo.
A manuscript posted before or during review.
Mean citations to a journal's recent items; a journal average.

worked_example.title: Will the first paper be out by the viva?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a four-year PhD of 48 months, with the first submission at month 24.
steps: Time left: 48 − 24 = 24 months.
The deck says first submission to publication takes 9 to 18 months with one journal.
With one rejection first it takes 18 to 30 months.
24 months sits inside the 18 to 30 range, so publication by the viva is possible but not assured.
worked_example.answer: 24 months remain; an outcome inside 18 to 30 months is likely.

mistakes: Choosing a journal by impact factor and ignoring whether it publishes papers like yours.
Checking a journal's claimed indexing on its own website instead of the index.
Paying an article processing charge when the green route would do.
Waiting passively after submission instead of starting the next paper.

recall.q: How many journals should the shortlist hold?
recall.a: Four, in order.

recall.q: Which three routes are free to the author?
recall.a: Green, diamond and preprint.

recall.q: What does One Nation One Subscription cover?
recall.a: It covers reading only, and the article processing charge is still yours.

recall.q: What should the cover letter contain?
recall.a: Title, question and main finding in numbers, fit, and all disclosures.

recall.q: What do journal metrics measure?
recall.a: A journal average that says nothing about the quality of your paper.

sections.title: Peer Review and Revision
sections.big_idea: Treat the referees' reports as **the most expert reading** your paper will get, and respond to every point.
in_plain_words: An editor decides after reading two or three unpaid referee reports; it is not a vote. Read the decision letter, put it aside for a day, then read it again with a pen and number every comment.

The response document quotes each comment in full, starts each reply with what you did and locates every change by page and table. Where a referee is wrong, show why and change the text anyway, since a misunderstanding means the paper misled.

Rejection is the normal outcome. Send the paper on within a month after fixing what the reports got right. Check proofs within 48 hours and referee in return, about three papers for each one you submit.

diagram.caption: the loop from submission to decision

key_terms.meaning: The editor wants the paper if the concerns can be met.
Rejection by the editor before referee review.
Point-by-point reply quoting each comment and locating each change.
A journal's published correction of its own error.
An author's published correction.

worked_example.title: Quantify the attrition gap
worked_example.setup: In the deck's response, attrition was 11.8% in treatment and 13.9% in control.
steps: Difference between arms: 13.9 − 11.8 = 2.1 percentage points.
The response also reports a p-value of 0.31 for the difference, which is not significant.
Bound the estimate (the deck uses Lee bounds) and report the effect range of 5.1 to 9.4 points.
Add a paragraph to results and a sentence to limitations, and cite the page.
worked_example.answer: A 2.1-point attrition gap, answered with bounds and located changes.

mistakes: Reading the letter once, emotionally, and starting revisions at once.
Quoting only part of a referee's comment in the response.
Resubmitting a rejected paper unchanged to the next journal.
Appealing on a difference of judgement instead of a demonstrable factual error.

recall.q: How many referees does a typical paper get?
recall.a: Two or three.

recall.q: What should you do first when two referees disagree?
recall.a: Follow the editor's steer; otherwise do what strengthens the argument and explain.

recall.q: When does an appeal succeed?
recall.a: When a referee's factual error that the editor relied on can be shown.

recall.q: How long do you have to return proofs?
recall.a: 48 hours.

recall.q: How many reviews does each submitted paper cost the community?
recall.a: Three.

sections.title: Authorship, Ethics and Practice
sections.big_idea: An author meets **all four ICMJE criteria**; declarations, AI disclosure and steady habits finish the job.
in_plain_words: The ICMJE criteria require substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, approval of the final version and accountability. Gift, ghost, guest and coercive authorship all break them. CRediT roles make the conversation concrete.

Order conventions differ by field, so agree in writing at the start. Every paper declares ethics approval, consent, registration, funding, competing interests, data, contributions and AI use. Keep the numbers in one file.

Generative tools cannot be authors and their use is disclosed. Habit is the method: short daily sessions and a writing group. A policy brief reverses the order of an article, and a fifteen-line checklist removes desk-rejection risk.

children.label: Gift
items: Head or supervisor added for rank

children.label: Coercive
items: Byline demanded for data or approval

diagram.caption: four ways the criteria are broken

key_terms.meaning: Four requirements, all of which an author must meet.
Fourteen contributor roles stated per author.
The person handling submission and queries; a job and carries no rank.
Where data and code are, or why they cannot be shared.
A 2 to 4 page version opening on the recommendation.

worked_example.title: Is this person an author?
worked_example.setup: Three people: a supervisor who only funded the project and supervised; a research assistant who analysed the data and drafted tables; a field enumerator who collected data.
steps: The deck says someone who is only 'supervision' and 'funding acquisition' does not meet the ICMJE criteria.
The assistant analysed and drafted, so check the other two criteria: final approval and accountability.
If all four are met, list them as an author, or they become a ghost author if left off.
The enumerator is named in the acknowledgements with permission, and paid.
worked_example.answer: The supervisor alone is not an author; the assistant is, if all four are met; the enumerator is thanked.

mistakes: Assuming the supervisor is always last author as a rule.
Leaving declaration numbers to be found three years later.
Pasting unpublished data into a tool that retains it.
Using AI for a claim, a reference or a result.

recall.q: How many ICMJE criteria must an author meet?
recall.a: All four.

recall.q: What does the deck say about economics author order?
recall.a: It is alphabetical, regardless of contribution.

recall.q: What is one-sentence AI disclosure?
recall.a: The tool, version, use, and that authors reviewed and take responsibility.

recall.q: How many items are on the checklist?
recall.a: Fifteen lines.

recall.q: What is the first book on the reading list?
recall.a: Booth, Colomb and Williams, The Craft of Research.

notes.2: Read the agenda in two halves. Sections 2 to 7 apply to any social-science genre, and sections 8 to 11 cover the process, written for researchers in South Asia. Find the stage you are at and start there, then return for the rest.
notes.4: The definition lists five things a reader should be able to check: the claim, the evidence, the reasoning, the place among other studies and room to disagree. If you have those five, the writing is academic. Long words and passive verbs add none of them.
notes.5: Pick the row that matches your reader before you write. The same study can fill four rows, yet each version has its own length and order. Relabelling a thesis chapter as an article leaves **3,000 words of literature** the journal does not want.
notes.6: Your reader reads the title, abstract, first figure and conclusion first, so put the claim there. Then give the draft to someone outside your sub-field and ask them to mark every sentence they read twice. Those **marked sentences are your edit list**.
notes.7: You probably learned from one of these two models. The essay teaches length and a late conclusion, and the report teaches bullets and floating recommendations. Keep the report's plain sentences and findings first, and add what both lack: reasoning a **stranger can check**.
notes.8: Short plain sentences work in your favour here, because a plain sentence reads as clear and an ornate one as strained. Keep Indian English forms you chose on purpose, and change only what stops the reader. Draft the argument first and the English second.
notes.9: Plan a pipeline, since drafting is the short part. Belcher's plan takes 12 weeks at about an hour a day, yet top economics journals took 24 to 30 months from submission to acceptance by the late 1990s. Keep papers **under review, in revision and in draft** at once.
notes.10: Read this as a map in six stages: argument, structure, prose, evidence, process, ethics. Sections 8 to 11 name the Indian regulations because most readers work under them. Use Systematic Reviews 101 for the review and Research Ethics 101 for consent.
notes.12: Locate your draft on these four steps. Most stalled drafts sit at the first or second, a topic or a question. Write the card sentence, 'This paper shows that X, because Y, which matters for Z', and **keep every old version** to see what you learned.
notes.13: Name your contribution before you write the introduction, using the left column. Each row also tells you what the paper must show: a better estimate must explain why earlier ones were doubtful. If your project fits only the 'not contributions' list, rethink it.
notes.14: Picture an hourglass: one wide paragraph on the problem, a long neck of data and results, then a wide close on what it means. The neck is where length is earned. Whatever your field, the **main result and its number** go in the introduction.
notes.15: List the referee's likely objections before drafting, then give each serious one its own paragraph, an analysis and a sentence saying how far it is answered. 'We acknowledge this limitation' answers nothing. Present in a seminar, because each question is a missing paragraph.
notes.16: Write the title in plain words that a search engine will match, and the abstract in 150 to 250 words with the result and its number. The abstract is quoted by people who never open the PDF, so **it must stand alone**. Write it last, then rewrite it first.
notes.17: Use the table as a drafting template: seven paragraphs, two to four pages. Paragraph 6 is where most rejections are decided, so name the two or three closest papers and say exactly what differs. Health and sociology journals prefer paragraphs 1 to 3 only.
notes.18: Draft the conclusion around what follows from the results. A policy implication names an actor, an action and the evidence for it. Match the verb to the evidence: **'shows' for the main result, 'suggests' for the mechanism**, 'is consistent with' for the untested story.
notes.20: Find your field's column and copy the shape of your target journal, which you learn by reading it. Whatever the headings, a reader must find the sample size, comparison group, main estimate and its confidence interval **in under a minute**.
notes.21: Write the setting section for the reader in Boston, and keep it to facts the argument uses. Then run the deck's test: delete a sentence, and if nothing later refers back to it, it was tourism. Each setting fact should return when you discuss **where the result might hold**.
notes.22: Use the table as a checklist, one row per paragraph. Table 1 is read more than any other, so every number in it should be reproducible from the replication package. The deck says the American Economic Association has required that since 2019.
notes.23: A methods section owes three things: the equation, the assumption that makes the coefficient an effect, and the evidence for that assumption. Most drafts have only the first. Qualitative work owes the same three. The standard is a **hostile expert getting your Table 2**.
notes.24: Open each results paragraph with the finding and its size, then point to the table. Watch four words: significant needs a level, effect claims causation, marginally significant means not significant, and any claim of robustness needs the checks listed. **Every prose number must match its table.**
notes.25: Work through the six steps and finish on limits. The comparison step is where your paper joins the literature, so say why your estimate differs from earlier ones. State each limitation with a **direction of bias**, since that tells the reader what to do with the number.
notes.26: Sort each item with one test: does a general reader need it to believe the main result? Confirming robustness checks and full tables go to the appendix, while the **one check that changes the answer** stays in the paper. Number appendix items and cite each from the text.
notes.27: Decide between monograph and three-paper thesis in year one, in writing, with your supervisor. The monograph carries one argument across chapters, and the three-paper form gives publishable papers. Check your university's ordinance either way, and read Dunleavy on structure.
notes.28: Write the outline as headings with one sentence under each, and make headings claims. After drafting, **reverse-outline**: one sentence beside each paragraph, then read only those. It takes an hour and finds structural problems that the prose hides.
notes.30: If your draft has one paragraph per paper in reading order, it is an annotated bibliography, and examiners will ask 'what is your argument?'. Organise by theme, finding or method, and end on a gap phrased as a **question your data can answer**.
notes.31: Read in three passes: triage in five minutes, structure in twenty, and close reading for the twenty papers nearest your question. Record each in fixed fields. A **synthesis matrix** with one row per study shows the structure of the review when you sort a column.
notes.32: Write each theme in three moves. Group states a claim about several studies. Explain says why they differ. Position shows where your study sits in the gap. The review can run four paragraphs or forty pages, and **the moves stay the same**.
notes.33: Add reports, working papers and government documents to your search, since much development evidence never reaches a journal. Appraise them like papers: design, sample, funder and whether the outcome was pre-specified. Cite the document behind a news item, **never the summary**.
notes.34: Ask what work your theory does. It should say which mechanisms to look for and what results would support or undermine it, as testable implications. Then run the test: name a result that would differ under another framework. If you cannot, cut the chapter.
notes.35: Set up saved searches and journal alerts in week one. One hour a fortnight keeps a four-year review current, while a month before submission does not. Re-run the search a month before you submit. Install **Zotero** early, because retyping 400 references in the last month brings errors.
notes.36: Use the table to set your review's length by genre, then check the target journal's recent articles. The widest gap is the Indian examiner's expectation of 25 to 60 pages for a monograph thesis against 1 to 2 pages in an economics article. Ask for two passed theses.
notes.38: Apply two rules: make the main characters the subjects and their actions the verbs. 'Enrolment rose after the transfer began' has both. Turn nominalisations back into verbs, keep subject and verb close, and **break any rule** before writing something barbarous.
notes.39: Put old information first and new information last. The start tells the reader what the sentence is about, and the end carries the stress. Check by reading the **last word of each sentence** in a paragraph. Write 'this effect', so the reader never has to guess.
notes.40: Use the four-part paragraph: claim, support, qualification, link. Test it by copying only the topic sentences into a new file and reading them in order. If they make no case, a paragraph is doing two jobs or none. Link with content, and skip stock connectives.
notes.41: Pick your verb from the row your evidence belongs to and use it once. Randomised, precise results earn 'shows', and correlations get 'is associated with'. Over-hedging signals you doubt your result, and under-hedging claims more than the evidence carries.
notes.42: After your first draft, search for each word in the left column and fix or cut it. Most drafts lose **10% of their length** and nothing else. Keep technical terms defined once, 'I' and 'we', short verbs, and a gloss for Indian terms on first use.
notes.43: Define each technical term in the text at first use, and keep abbreviations to five or six. A term is jargon only when the reader does not need it. Spell out sector abbreviations such as MEL and ToC for a journal, and borrow the **target journal's words**.
notes.44: Draft and revise on different days. Write fast from the outline with placeholders, then revise in five passes with one question each. Read aloud, wait a week if the deadline allows, and cut 10% at the end. **Never edit the only copy.**
notes.45: Ask for specific comments, such as 'Where did you stop believing me?', and treat every comment as data about a reader, even a wrong one. Do not defend the draft in the meeting. If your supervisor corrects only grammar, ask whether **the contribution is enough**.
notes.46: Pick your tool by who must read your file. Word with Zotero is the safe default for an Indian social-science PhD, and LaTeX suits economics. Quarto removes hand-copying of numbers when results come from R or Stata. Use a grammar checker for mechanics only.
notes.48: Round in prose and keep decimals in tables. Always give the base and the precision, and tell percent from percentage points: 75% to 81% is 6 points, or 8 percent. Say 'tripled' or give both numbers, because readers misread 'increased by 200%'.
notes.49: Let the title carry the outcome and sample, and the note carry everything needed to read the table alone. In a regression table, order columns from the sparest to the fullest and put the coefficient of interest first. **Generate the table from code**, never retype.
notes.50: Use a table when readers look numbers up, and a figure when they should see a pattern. Four coefficients belong in a table, and an event study in a figure. Give every plotted estimate its interval, put **one message in the title** and export vector or 300 dpi.
notes.51: After each displayed equation, define every symbol in order, name the coefficient of interest and state the error structure. Number displayed equations and use one notation across all chapters. With one equation, words can do the job; with ten, use LaTeX.
notes.52: Read Table 1 as a referee would: does n match the text, are the means plausible, are groups balanced, is the baseline outcome mean here? The figures are illustrative. Skip stars on a balance table, since with twenty variables **one will look significant by chance**.
notes.53: Treat a quotation as an exhibit: say what it shows, give an identifier, then say how it supports the claim and how typical it was. Give counts in place of 'several'. A themes-by-group matrix and a participant table make qualitative work **checkable**.
notes.54: Build the replication package before you submit, because that is when errors surface. It needs data or instructions, one script from raw data to the last figure, a README and software versions. Deposit it with a DOI and **test it on a clean machine**.
notes.56: A citation lets the reader check a claim, credits the person and places your paper. Cite every fact that is not yours and not common knowledge, and when in doubt, cite. Cite what you read, and write 'X, cited in Y' for second-hand sources.
notes.57: The journal picks the style, so use a reference manager and make completeness your job. Each entry needs authors, year, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI, plus a URL and access date for online-only items. Use the table to match style to field.
notes.58: Learn the tiers: up to 10% no penalty, above 10% to 40% revise within six months, above 40% to 60% debarred for a year, above 60% registration cancelled. Then remember **the score only finds matching strings**; plagiarism is the act, and it can occur at 3%.
notes.59: Tell the editor in the cover letter about any thesis, working paper, companion paper or conference version. Reusing a methods paragraph with a citation is generally tolerated, a reused introduction is not. Salami slicing splits one study thin, and duplicate submission sends one paper to two journals.
notes.60: Paraphrase from memory: read the passage, close it, write what it says, then reopen it to check and add the citation. Writing with the source open produces **patchwriting**, which is plagiarism even when cited. Quote only when the exact words are the evidence.
notes.61: Fabrication invents results and falsification changes them, and undisclosed specification search is falsification. Report what was pre-specified, what was exploratory and how much you tried. A registered **pre-analysis plan** makes a null result publishable. Keep the raw file for every figure.
notes.62: Run each kind of material through the table. Short quotations with citation are fine, redrawn figures are usually fine, and a reproduced figure needs permission unless openly licensed. Read what you sign, since a copyright transfer gives the publisher the paper.
notes.63: Follow the six steps from capture to verify. The last one catches what reference software adds: a preprint where a published version exists, duplicate entries, a wrong page range. Check every reference a language model suggests against its **DOI**, because it can invent plausible ones.
notes.65: Use the table to see the stages you pass through, then get your university's ordinance in the first month and read it twice, since it governs chapter lists, limits and format. The 2022 rules dropped the national publication requirement, though a university may still require it.
notes.66: Write the proposal as the thesis in miniature, with the question first and methods following from it. Address feasibility directly: access, cost, time and ethical clearance. Add a timeline by semester. **Nothing written here is wasted**, since it becomes chapters 2 and 3.
notes.67: Manage the supervisor relationship with a one-page agenda before meetings and a one-page note after. Ask for feedback on structure early and on prose late. If it goes wrong, **document dates** of drafts sent and meetings requested before using the committee route.
notes.68: Use the table as a format check before submission, because a thesis returned for corrections loses two months. Build the template in year one from your ordinance and two recently passed theses. Generate the contents list automatically and keep one reference style.
notes.69: Write for two named examiners who read the abstract, contents, introduction and conclusion first. Expect award, minor corrections, major revision or reject. For corrections, do all of them, tabulate where, and have your supervisor certify it. Read a major-revision report for **argument or evidence**.
notes.70: Prepare the viva as a defence of your own work: a presentation that follows the hourglass, answers to the examiners' written concerns and a mock viva. In answers, listen to the whole question, pause, answer briefly and stop. **Write down the corrections** before you leave.
notes.71: Remember that your thesis becomes a public document on Shodhganga. Pseudonymise participants and get permission for copyrighted figures. Tell journals when an article derives from the deposited thesis. Search Shodhganga in year one, since your question may already have been asked.
notes.72: Plan the article path in year one: choose the form, write the first empirical chapter as an article in year two, and submit in year three. Cutting is how a chapter becomes an article. If no argument is left after cutting, **the chapter was a report**.
notes.74: Choose by fit first, then reach, speed and cost. Shortlist four journals in order and write for the first. Journals that appear three times or more in your reference list are candidates. If the last two issues hold nothing like your paper, **it is the wrong journal**.
notes.75: Treat the table as a starting list for development and social-science outlets, and it is no ranking. Notice what suits which method: Journal of Development Studies takes qualitative and mixed methods, Journal of Development Economics expects identification, and EPW reaches policy readers. Check each journal's aims and scope.
notes.76: Check a journal on DOAJ, Scopus or Web of Science themselves, never on the journal's own site. Warning signs include flattering invitations, fees revealed after acceptance, unknown 'impact factors' and acceptance in a week. A paper there **can be held against you** and cannot be republished.
notes.77: For most South Asian authors the practical route is green plus a preprint: free and compliant with nearly every funder. Pay a gold fee only when a funder pays or your readers cannot otherwise reach the paper. One Nation One Subscription covers reading, so **the charge stays yours**.
notes.78: Post a preprint when the paper is ready for criticism, and post the version you submitted. Check the journal's policy first. Cite preprints as preprints, and update to the published version. An institutional series gives a number, date and RePEc place that a job market can cite.
notes.79: Keep the cover letter to half a page, addressed to the editor by name, with the main finding in numbers and every disclosure. Anonymise for double-blind review and follow the format instructions exactly. **The day you submit, start the next paper.**
notes.80: Every metric averages a journal and says nothing about your paper. Use the table to learn what each measures and what it must not be used for. Know the numbers your promotion committee uses. An impact factor to five decimals from an unknown body is a **predatory signal**.
notes.81: Apply the predatory-journal checks to special issues too. A guest editor who knows the field is a good sign, and an email from an unknown journal is not. Publish the article before the chapter. A book from a thesis needs about a year of rewriting.
notes.82: Use the table to set expectations: 9 to 18 months from first submission with one journal, and 18 to 30 including one rejection, which is the usual case. You control the quality of the first submission and the speed of revision, so **keep three papers moving at once**.
notes.84: Follow the paper through six stages and notice that the editor decides, which is not a vote. Referees are unpaid colleagues reading for what is wrong, so their report is the **most expert reading** your paper will get. Become a referee early; it teaches how papers are judged.
notes.85: Read the decision letter once, put it away for a day, then read it with a pen. The editor's emphasis decides. A referee who misunderstood was misled by your text, so **fix the paper**. Number every comment in a table that becomes the response document.
notes.86: Quote every comment in full, start each reply with what you did, and locate each change by page and table. Agree where the referee is right. Where they are wrong, show why with evidence and change the text so the next reader does not err. The response is often longer than the paper.
notes.87: Run the analyses first, then revise the text, and revise the introduction and abstract last. Send a tracked-changes copy and make no unexplained edits. When referees disagree, choose what strengthens the argument, say so, and put the other version in the appendix. Meet the deadline, or ask before it passes.
notes.88: Rejection is normal at most journals. Read the reports after a day, fix what they got right and send the paper to the next journal within a month. Never resubmit unchanged. Appeal only for a demonstrable factual error, and **keep a log** of outcomes.
notes.89: Return proofs in 48 hours, checking every number, name, reference and the copy-editor's changes, because this is the last correction without a published erratum. Then post the accepted manuscript, update your profiles, send a plain-language summary and deposit the replication package.
notes.90: Referee in five steps: read twice, summarise, list two or three major concerns with fixes, list minor points, and recommend. A good report is specific, constructive and about two pages, and it stays confidential. The deck says to referee **three papers** for each one you submit.
notes.92: Test each possible author against all four ICMJE criteria; all four must be met. Know the four bad forms: gift, ghost, guest and coercive. CRediT roles make the conversation concrete. Name field staff in the acknowledgements with permission, and pay them.
notes.93: Agree author order in writing at the start, then revisit it when the draft exists. Economics lists alphabetically, health fields order by contribution with the senior author last, and teams use a contribution note. **Corresponding author is a job** and carries no rank.
notes.94: Collect approval, registration and grant numbers in one file at the start of the project. The table lists what a paper declares: ethics, consent, registration, funding, competing interests, data, contributions and AI use. A missing declaration can mean desk rejection and a false one is misconduct.
notes.95: A language model cannot be an author, and its use is disclosed in one sentence naming tool, version, purpose and your review. Use it for tasks you can check, such as language editing. **Never use it for claims**, references, results or images, and never paste unpublished data into tools that retain it.
notes.96: Write in short scheduled sessions: thirty minutes at the same time every working day, before email. Track minutes, stop mid-paragraph and join a writing group. If blocked, tell perfectionism, fear and a missing argument apart. If the claim card cannot be written, **the block is in the thinking**.
notes.97: Reverse the order for a policy reader: recommendation and number first, evidence in a page, method in a box, cost and actor last. Write the brief **after the paper is accepted**. Round numbers, hedge as the paper does, and cite the paper for anyone who wants the apparatus.
notes.98: Treat the fifteen lines as your final gate and tick each only after checking it in the files. Passing all fifteen removes every reason for desk rejection within your control. Work in the order shown: argument and structure first, evidence and apparatus second.
notes.99: Start with Booth, Colomb and Williams, which the deck says everyone should own. Add by need: Williams and Bizup for sentences, Belcher for a schedule, Dunleavy or Murray for the thesis. Then read the UGC regulations and your **university's ordinance** twice.
